paras: The Johnston's election-day shooting took place on November 2, 1880, at the polling place at Johnston's in Edgefield County, South Carolina, when men at the poll opened fire on a crowd of Black voters, killing one Black man and wounding several others. South Carolina papers blamed the Black voters, while national wires carried the killing as an 'election riot' at Edgefield with counts of the wounded that ranged from one to thirteen. Months later the killing was cited in a contested congressional election as evidence of Democratic violence that went unpunished.

According to a dispatch sent from Johnston's that day, seven or eight hundred Black voters crowded the poll so closely that the officers could hardly receive the ballots. The same dispatch said trouble had been expected and that men from Trenton and Batesburg had been telegraphed to come to 'our relief'.

The local account said things went quietly until about 10 o'clock, when a Black man struck a white man on the head with a stick and drew a pistol. The men around the poll then 'commenced firing with guns and pistols'; one Black man was killed and several were reported mortally wounded, while no whites were hurt. An Augusta wire sent the same day gave a different cause, saying the Black voters had tried to seize the ballot-box, and counted one killed and three wounded.

Further trouble was expected that night, and a hundred men from Augusta and Batesburg were said to be on their way to the precinct. Returns from Edgefield Court-House, by contrast, reported that everything there had passed off quietly.

No report of an inquest or of arrests appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named the man killed, the wounded, or the men who fired. In April 1881 a Columbia dispatch summarizing testimony in Robert Smalls's contest of G. D. Tillman's election said that 400 to 500 Black Republicans had been kept from voting at Johnstone's. The same summary stated that a Black man had been killed at the poll and that 'no efforts have been made by the State to bring the murderers to justice.'

South Carolina papers framed the shooting as the Black voters' doing: the Pickens Sentinel wrote that 'the negroes precipitated a difficulty', and the Baptist Courier listed the attempt 'to seize the ballot box at Johnston's' as one of the few disturbances in a peaceful election. The Anderson Intelligencer printed the local dispatch under the headline 'South Carolina Safe' among Democratic returns.

Outside the state, the Augusta wire ran on November 3 in Chicago, St. Paul and Sacramento, the St. Paul Daily Globe heading it 'The South Carolina Row.' A second wire dated Edgefield, November 4, appeared as 'Serious Election Riot' in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and 'Fatal Election Riot' in the Los Angeles Herald. A Columbia dispatch giving thirteen wounded reached Midwestern weeklies, where the Chillicothe Crisis placed it in a crime column.

Partisan papers used the report for their own ends. The Wichita City Eagle wrote sarcastically that 'They only' killed one and wounded thirteen 'at Edgeville', while the Democratic State Rights Democrat of Oregon reprinted the Edgefield dispatch to charge the Oregonian with inconsistency about Southern voting. In 1881 the Washington National Republican placed the killing in a catalogue of 'Democratic fraud, intimidation, and violence' drawn from the Smalls contest.

Every account of how the shooting began came from the white Democratic side, and they differed: a blow with a stick and a drawn pistol in the local dispatch, an attempt on the ballot-box in the Augusta wire and the Baptist Courier. Counts of the wounded also varied, from 'several mortally wounded' in the local dispatch and three in the Augusta wire to eleven or thirteen in later wires, with the Los Angeles Herald printing one. The same-day local dispatch is the closest account, but it gives no number for the wounded.

reader.title: Johnston's election-day shooting
bases: Men at the Johnston's poll opened fire with guns and pistols on a crowd of several hundred Black voters, killing one Black man and wounding several, with no whites hurt (A7, A3, A26).

A local Johnston's dispatch, an Augusta wire, a Columbia dispatch, two South Carolina weeklies and later election-contest testimony agree that one Black man was killed at the Johnston's poll on election day, though they differ on the wounded (A7, A3, A17, A14, A16, A26).

accounts.label: Local Johnston's dispatch
accounts.gist: Seven or eight hundred Black voters crowded the poll; about 10 o'clock a Black man struck a white man with a stick and drew a pistol, the men around began firing, one Black man was killed and several mortally wounded, and no whites were hurt.

accounts.label: Augusta wire
accounts.gist: A riot between whites and Black voters at 'Johnson's' after the Black voters tried to seize the ballot-box; one killed and three wounded.

accounts.label: Edgefield and Columbia wires
accounts.gist: One Black man killed and eleven (or thirteen) wounded in an 'election riot' at Edgefield on election day.

accounts.label: Election-contest testimony
accounts.gist: Sworn testimony in the Smalls-Tillman contest, as summarized by a Columbia dispatch, said 400-500 Black Republicans were kept from voting at Johnstone's, a Black man was killed there, and the state made no effort to punish the killers.

framing.detail: South Carolina papers said 'the negroes precipitated a difficulty' or tried 'to seize the ballot box', presenting the shooting as the only disturbance in an otherwise peaceful election.
National papers ran the Augusta wire as 'The South Carolina Row' and the Edgefield wire as 'Serious Election Riot' or 'Fatal Election Riot' without comment.
The Wichita City Eagle sarcastically wrote that Democrats 'only' killed one and wounded thirteen, and the Republican National Republican cited the killing as Democratic violence that went unpunished.
The Democratic State Rights Democrat reprinted the Edgefield dispatch only to accuse the Oregonian of inconsistency about Southern voting.

conflicts.note: The local Johnston's dispatch, written the same day, is the closest account but gives no number; the larger later wire figures cannot be traced to a named source.
